\section[colloquor, colloquī]{colloquor, colloquī — to talk together}

\label{lesson:LA-C201-colloquor}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for to refuse, then the Latin for to fly about.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: colloquor, colloquī}
\textbf{colloquor, colloquī} — \textquotedblleft{}to talk together\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{colloquor} is \emph{con-}, \textquotedblleft{}together\textquotedblright{}, with \emph{loquor}, \textquotedblleft{}to speak\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1). English \emph{colloquial} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[trādō, trādere]{trādō, trādere — to hand over}

\label{lesson:LA-C201-trado}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for to fly about, then the Latin for to talk together.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: trādō, trādere}
\textbf{trādō, trādere} — \textquotedblleft{}to hand over\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{trādō} is contracted from \emph{trāns}, \textquotedblleft{}across\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{dō}, \textquotedblleft{}to give\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short): to hand across. English \emph{tradition} and \emph{traitor} come from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[corrigō, corrigere]{corrigō, corrigere — to straighten, to correct}

Before the new one: say the Latin for to talk together, then the Latin for to hand over.

\subsection*{You'll want to know: corrigō, corrigere}
\textbf{corrigō, corrigere} — \textquotedblleft{}to straighten, to correct\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{corrigō} is \emph{regō}, \textquotedblleft{}to keep straight\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), with \emph{con-}, \textquotedblleft{}thoroughly\textquotedblright{}: to make fully straight.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[celebrō, celebrāre]{celebrō, celebrāre — to celebrate}

\label{lesson:LA-C201-celebro}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for to hand over, then the Latin for to straighten.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: celebrō, celebrāre}
\textbf{celebrō, celebrāre} — \textquotedblleft{}to celebrate\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{celebrō} is built on \emph{celeber}, \textquotedblleft{}crowded, much visited\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short): to throng a place, then to honour it with crowds.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[persequor, persequī]{persequor, persequī — to pursue}

\label{lesson:LA-C201-persequor}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for to straighten, then the Latin for to celebrate.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: persequor, persequī}
\textbf{persequor, persequī} — \textquotedblleft{}to pursue\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{persequor} is \emph{per}, \textquotedblleft{}through\textquotedblright{}, with \emph{sequor}, \textquotedblleft{}to follow\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1). \emph{sequor} is usually traced to Proto-Indo-European \emph{*sekw-}, \textquotedblleft{}to follow\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1).
\end{cousinweb}
